# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files, comment-only changes, and history-keeping updates (a version bump, a changelog or `VERSIONS.md` row).
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.

Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.

Use from a canon when a project's evidence shows a facet its shelf does not yet home — the curation stages' pack-writing method, and an owner's when asking what a project has taught the shelf.

Use when designing a larger element (the brief is authored then), when filing a migration plan's chain (the retrospective is its last link), when a merge completes a design-doc'd element, or when defining a new retrospective class for a pack, a repo, or the fleet.

You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.

Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

---
name: writing-pack-prose
description: How pack prose is written — RULES.md rules, SKILL.md bodies and check text in a Claudinite pack, local or canon — brevity, structure, triggerability, findability, and the per-pack references doc that carries each rule's rationale. Use before writing or editing any pack's RULES.md or SKILL.md, or when landing a lesson as prose.
---

# Writing pack prose

How the prose in a Claudinite pack is written — the rules in a `RULES.md`, the body of a
`SKILL.md`, the `failureMessage`/`what`/`fix` text of a check — in a repo's own local packs and
in the shared canon alike. What *qualifies* as a rule and which mechanism carries it is
[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)'s territory; instruction files outside a
pack (a consumer repo's CLAUDE.md, a convention doc) are the `authoring-agent-docs` skill's.

**Start from the foundation:** read the "Write each rule" section of
[authoring-agent-docs](../../../basics/skills/authoring-agent-docs/SKILL.md) first — its
principles (concrete enough to verify, motivation stated, what to do rather than what not to,
the right altitude, emphasis reserved) bind pack prose too. This skill is the pack-specific
layer on top of them, and doesn't restate them.

## The ration

Every rule in a `RULES.md` is paid for by every session in every repo that declares the pack,
forever, whether or not it ever applies — so prose is rationed, and the ration is small.

- **One sentence per rule, near 40 words**: the trigger, the directive, and a consequence
  clause only where the rule cannot be applied without it. A candidate that needs a paragraph
  to land has not been understood well enough to be a rule yet.
- **An extraction pass adds at most two rules.** If more candidates clear the bar, write the
  two strongest and drop the rest — they will recur if they were real.
- **Split a rule that carries two situations.** Each situation is its own rule with its own
  trigger.
- A `SKILL.md` loads only when its activity is under way, so it may carry procedure at length —
  but it is still rationed by the same test: every line must change what the reader does.
  Method, steps and decision points belong there; anything a session must know *without*
  loading it belongs in `RULES.md` or a check, and rationale belongs in the references doc
  below.

## Shape a rule so it fires

- **Keying a rule to its trigger** — open with the act the reader is performing, not the state
  of the world the rule applies to. Nobody notices that "a value is unknown"; they notice they
  are writing an encoder. A rule keyed to a state never fires, because nothing brings the
  reader to it.
- **Keying a rule the reader reaches while debugging** — name the symptom that sends them
  looking ("A fetch to a host you listed failing in-browser"), not the act that caused it. By
  the time the rule is wanted the act is over, and the symptom is what they can see.
- **Keying a rule that corrects a misconception** — name what the reader wants ("Wanting
  `import`/`export` in extension code"), not the wrong move they might make ("Reaching for a
  bundler"). Someone who doesn't yet know the move is wrong won't recognise themselves in it.
- **Phrasing that trigger** — use the words the reader would use for the situation, and put
  them first and in bold, so the rule is findable by scanning the left margin alone.
- **Choosing the unit** — one block per situation, not one bullet per rule. A reader arrives
  holding a problem, so give them the whole decision in one place rather than a cross-reference
  to three neighbouring bullets.
- **Splitting a rule that only makes sense after the one above it** — don't. If the subject
  needs a "that" pointing back ("Writing that record"), it is a clause of the rule above, not a
  situation of its own. Split when a reader could arrive at the second rule without the first.
- **Separating the blocks** — one blank line between rules. The block is what a reader lands on,
  and an unbroken run of bullets makes them scan lines instead; the separation costs one token.
- **Ordering a file of many rules** — past roughly fifteen, group them under headings naming the
  surface each concerns, so a reader scans headings before subjects. A flat list that long makes
  every bold subject do the work one heading would.
- **Grouping that separates two rules which qualify each other** — add an explicit pointer from
  the general rule to its exception, or the general one reads as unconditional. That pointer is
  the one sentence a rewrite may add that its source didn't have; name it as an addition when
  you report the change.
- **Ordering the clauses** — the default first, then the `if you can't` fallback, then
  `consider` for an optional aid, then the `don't` that the earlier clauses make unnecessary.
- **Choosing modality** — grade it per clause and claim no more than the rule needs. Keep
  `never` and `always` for the genuinely absolute and reach for `prefer`, `avoid` or `rather
  than` otherwise; escalating a `don't` into a `never` changes the rule rather than rewording
  it.
- **Naming a mechanism** — name the check, helper or skill that owns the mechanics, and stop.
  Its parameters, options and failure modes live with it, and restating them here is a copy
  that goes stale. The exception is a mechanism you are telling the reader to *run*, below.
- **Telling the reader to *run* something** — ship the literal invocation in a fenced block, not
  the file's name. The reader is composing a call rather than looking a mechanism up, so a bare
  filename buys a probe every time — the `--help` that prints nothing, then the `cat`, then a
  hand-built command. (1)
- **Closing a block** — say what the other clauses make unnecessary ("don't also comment the
  duplication — the guard covers it"), so nobody adds belt-and-braces.
- **Keeping an exception** — an exception that changes what the reader would do is part of the
  rule; one that only reassures is padding.
- **Cutting a rule's prose** — drop rationale that only restates the rule, examples that
  re-express it, and mechanics another document owns. Keep the motivation itself: a consequence
  the reader needs in order to apply the rule under pressure earns its clause; rationale the
  reader doesn't need at act time goes to the references doc below.
- **Auditing a file of rules that already exists** — take each rule and ask what a reader would
  get wrong without it. Fold the one whose subject points back at its neighbour; cut the one another
  pack already carries, the one a check now enforces (keeping only the half the check can't see),
  and the one whose mechanism has since been retired — a rule naming code that no longer exists
  teaches a world the reader won't find.
- **Rewriting an existing rule** — carry the source's own strength forward. A rewrite must not
  weaken a rule, and it must not strengthen one either.

## The references doc — where a rule's rationale lives

A pack keeps **one** `references.md` beside its `RULES.md`, servicing all of the pack's prose
files and its checks. It exists for maintenance and review — the periodic pass that asks
whether a rule still earns its place needs the reason it was written — never for daily agentic
work: no rule sends its reader there, and no session loads it.

- **Adding a rule that has a rationale** — write the brief rule in `RULES.md` (or the skill),
  and put the reason in `references.md`. End the rule with the bare marker — `… never a
  filesystem walk. (3)` — and nothing else: don't name the references file, don't link it,
  don't ask the reader to follow anything. Not every rule needs one; a rule whose reason is
  self-evident from its consequence clause carries no marker.
- **Writing the entry** — one bullet per entry, keyed by the citing file's own namespace:
  `- **(RULES-3)** <reason>` for a rule in `RULES.md`, `- **(<skill-name>-3)** <reason>` for a
  line in that skill's `SKILL.md`; the marker in the prose file stays the bare `(3)` and
  resolves within its own file's namespace. Write the reason so a future review can **reaffirm
  the rule from it**: what would have to be true for the rule to be retired.
  - A **workaround** explains the issue with not using it, with the evidence (the failing run,
    the error, the measured cost).
  - A **technology guideline** cites the original documentation it derives from.
  - An **owner decision** carries the language of the request that set it.
- **Numbering** — numbers are stable identifiers, not positions: the next entry takes its
  file's next unused number, a removed entry leaves a gap, and nothing ever renumbers (a
  renumber breaks every marker at once). One entry may serve several rules in its file; a rule
  may cite several entries (`(3, 7)`).
- **A check's rationale** — the entry points at the check, since a declaration admits no
  comment and no new key: `- **(check:growth-write-scope)** <reason>`, same reaffirmation
  standard. There is no marker on the check side.
- **Removing a rule or check** — remove its entry in the same change, unless another rule
  still cites it.

The `references-integrity` check holds the mechanism together: every marker must resolve to an
entry in the pack's own `references.md`, and every `check:` entry must name a check the pack
still carries. The `rule-revalidation` task is the mechanism's consumer — it reaffirms
referenced rules and checks against their recorded reasons on its weekly pass.

## Migrating an existing pack onto the references doc

An existing pack — a repo's local pack, or a shared canon pack worked on canon-side (a member
never edits the mounted canon) — migrates opportunistically, one pack per pass, whenever a pass
is already editing it. An unmarked rule stays valid forever, so there is no fleet sweep to
force and no straggler to chase; the check only judges markers that exist.

1. **Create `references.md`** beside the pack's `RULES.md` on its first entry, not before.
2. **Work each rule**: keep the act-time consequence clause inline; move review-only rationale —
   the evidence story, inline issue ids, a cost the reader doesn't need mid-act — into an entry
   and end the rule with its marker. Shrink-only on the rules side: a rule may lose review-only
   rationale in this pass, never gain text.
3. **Recover the missing reasons from history, source-first**: for a rule that states no reason,
   read the commit that added it and that commit's PR and issue *before* re-reading the rule —
   derive the entry from the source, then diff against what the rule implied. The commit
   message, PR body and issue discussion are where this corpus already keeps a rule's evidence.
4. **Never invent an entry.** A rule whose reason can't be recovered stays unmarked — an audit
   or the `rule-revalidation` pass judges whether it still earns its place; a plausible-sounding
   fabricated rationale would let a future review reaffirm a rule on false grounds.
5. **Cover the checks** worth reaffirming with `check:` entries the same way, from their `why`
   text and their adding commit's PR.

## Evidence

The commit and its PR remain the archive — dates, session ids, quoted exchanges and the story
of the incident live there, never in the rule. What the references doc takes from them is only
the **reaffirmable core**: the reason and the minimum evidence a future review needs to re-test
it. Keep a measurement inline in the rule only where the number *is* the argument — a cost the
reader wouldn't believe stated qualitatively.

Migrates the shared canon packs onto the `writing-pack-prose` references convention (#1560), per its own migration procedure: shrink-only on the prose side, evidence recovered from what the prose already recorded, nothing invented.

## What moved

Six packs gain a `references.md` and bump their version:

- **basics** — `verify-in-production` sheds its six inline incident narratives (#1121, #1460, the five executor-batch parks, the cross-repo scope-denial parks, the hand-set label incidents #1220/#1265, and #1160's stale-retry), `do-later` its #1160 citation, `writing-tests` its three worked-example parentheticals (#429, #310, the hostname-apex case) — each rule keeps its act-time consequence and ends with a bare `(n)` marker; the evidence lives in the entries. A `check:` entry covers `declared-check-spec-keys` (#1400's fleet-lane trade).
- **claudinite-growth** — `unattended-agents`' three worked-example parentheticals, `writing-tasks`' design-doc pointer (#394), and `writing-pack-prose`'s own fenced-command measurement move to entries; a `check:` entry covers `task-md-only-when-agentic` (#1055).
- **claudinite-canon-curation** — both skills' #385 citations move to entries; a `check:` entry covers `pack-version-claimed-once` (#1482).
- **claudinite-lifecycle** — `adopt-claudinite`'s #1167 citation moves to an entry; `check:` entries cover `conformance-work-scope` (#939) and `rules-index-current` (#807).
- **aws-sam**, **chrome-extension** — `references.md` only, covering `handler-path` (#136, reaffirmable against esbuild's `outbase` documentation) and `declarative-content-set-icon` (#777, reaffirmable against a current Chrome).

One mechanism fix rode along as its own commit: `references-integrity`'s `CHECK_ENTRY`/`CHECK_IDS` patterns could not represent a slashed check id (`aws-sam/handler-path`), so such an entry sat inert — widened, red-first with a new fixture test.

## What deliberately did not move

- The technology packs' inline failure modes (macos, headless-browser, static-website, firebase, flutter, node, web-speech, web-scraping, html, leaflet) are **act-time consequence clauses** the convention keeps inline — examined, left unmarked. Measurements that *are* the argument (static-website's 0-byte timezone fix, the 6% join rate) stay inline per the skill's Evidence section.
- Rules with no recoverable rationale stay unmarked — the convention is opt-in per rule and never invents an entry.
- Checks guarding repo-internal structure get no `check:` entries: the tree settles them, and `rule-revalidation` scopes them out. Covered checks are the ones whose premise could lapse (platform behaviour, incident-born workarounds).

## Verification

- New slashed-id test seen red before the fix, green after; suite `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')`: 2931/2931 pass.
- `references-integrity` run against the real tree: 0 findings, and proven to bite on a deliberately dangling `(99)` marker before restoring.
- `check_the_world`: 0 blocking; 87 advisories before and after — none introduced.

import subprocess, re, json, sys

def sh(*a):
    return subprocess.run(a, capture_output=True, text=True).stdout

paths = ['packs/','.claudinite/']
commits = sh('git','log','--format=%H','--','packs/*/RULES.md','.claudinite/local/packs/*/RULES.md','packs/*/skills/*/SKILL.md','.claudinite/local_packs/*/RULES.md').split()
out=[]
for c in commits:
    parent = sh('git','rev-parse',c+'^').strip()
    if not parent or parent.startswith('fatal'): continue
    diff = sh('git','diff','--unified=0',parent,c,'--','packs/*/RULES.md','.claudinite/local/packs/*/RULES.md','packs/*/skills/*/SKILL.md','.claudinite/local_packs/*/RULES.md')
    cur_old_file=None; oldlines=None; ln=None
    for line in diff.split('\n'):
        if line.startswith('--- '):
            p=line[4:]
            cur_old_file = None if p=='/dev/null' else p[2:]
            oldlines = sh('git','show',f'{parent}:{cur_old_file}').split('\n') if cur_old_file else None
        elif line.startswith('@@'):
            m=re.match(r'@@ -(\d+)(?:,(\d+))? \+',line)
            ln=int(m.group(1)); cnt=int(m.group(2) or 1)
            removed=[]
        elif line.startswith('-') and not line.startswith('---') and oldlines is not None:
            removed_text=line[1:]
            # nearest preceding bold trigger
            idx=ln-1
            subj=None
            for j in range(min(idx,len(oldlines)-1),-1,-1):
                mm=re.match(r'\s*-\s+\*\*(.+?)\*\*',oldlines[j])
                if mm: subj=mm.group(1); break
                if oldlines[j].startswith('#'): break
            out.append({'commit':c[:8],'file':cur_old_file,'line':ln,'subject':subj,'text':removed_text})
            ln+=1
        elif line.startswith(' ') or line.startswith('+'):
            pass
json.dump(out,open(sys.argv[1],'w'),indent=0)
print(len(out))
EOF

import json,re,subprocess,os,sys
rem=json.load(open(sys.argv[1]))
def head(f):
    if not os.path.exists(f): return None
    return open(f).read()
cache={}
sig=re.compile(r'#\d{2,4}|because|otherwise|silently|spent|cost|wedge|measured|minutes|hours|\d+%|proved|turned out|we (?:once|had)|incident|regression', re.I)
cands={}
for r in rem:
    f=r['file']
    if not f: continue
    if f not in cache: cache[f]=head(f)
    txt=cache[f]
    if txt is None: continue  # file gone today
    subj=r['subject']
    if not subj: continue
    if f'**{subj}**' not in txt: continue  # rule gone
    if not sig.search(r['text']): continue
    if len(r['text'].strip())<20: continue
    cands.setdefault((f,subj),[]).append(r)
print(len(cands))
with open(sys.argv[2],'w') as o:
    for (f,subj),rs in sorted(cands.items()):
        o.write(f'\n### {f} :: {subj}\n')
        for r in rs:
            o.write(f"  [{r['commit']}] {r['text'].strip()}\n")
EOF

It can only fail when someone changes the value **on purpose**, so it catches no defect and instead taxes every deliberate change with a mirrored edit — and, worse, teaches that the value is load-bearing prose to be restated, which is how one setting ends up copied into a comment, a worker doc, a README table and a test, so flipping it becomes a five-file diff. input.body:
Follow-up to #1564/#1565, which migrated the shared packs onto the `writing-pack-prose` references convention using the rationale those files still carried. Rationale that earlier passes had already **deleted** is not in the working tree at all — it only exists in the change history.

Recover it: mine the repo's full history for rationale removed from a `RULES.md` or `SKILL.md` whose rule still stands today, verify each recovered reason against the commit/PR/issue it came from, and land it as `references.md` entries with markers on the rules that own them. Never invent an entry where nothing is recoverable.

{"number":919,"title":"Delete the two pack-entry config validators (and the seam that briefly replaced them)","body":"Reworked on the owner's call: a bespoke validation vocabulary is the wrong shape for config, whichever end it is authored at. The `configSchema` manifest seam this branch first added is reverted whole, and the two coded validators it was converting are **deleted** rather than moved. The net diff is deletions only.

## Gone

| rule | was |
|---|---|
| `growth-config` | `packs/grow_with_claudinite/config-check.mjs` — the entry config's shape (`retention_days`, `promote`, `pack_paths`) |
| `product-wiki-config-guard` | `packs/product-wiki/config-guard.mjs` — "this pack takes no config" |

Neither pack codes a rule any longer; `product-wiki`'s checks are now entirely its `declared-checks.json`. Also reverted: `engine/pack_loader/config-schema.mjs`, its wiring in `pack-schema.mjs`, its tests, the `copyLoader` test-fixture helper, and the `versioned-local` rehearsal fixture's `configSchema`.

## What this costs, stated plainly

A malformed `grow_with_claudinite` entry — `retention_days: "10"`, a typo'd key — is now silent: the retention sweep reads an unusable value and does nothing, and nothing says so. Same for a config object on a `product-wiki` entry, which the pack ignores. That is the accepted trade of removing the checks; if the shape should be enforced at all, it belongs to a schema over `.claudinite-checks.json` itself (a real JSON Schema the file points at with `$schema`), not to per-pack rules — that would be its own issue, and I have not opened one.

No member is reddened by the deletion: nothing validates rule ids in settings, so an existing `"growth-config": "off"` simply goes inert.

## Verification

`node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` — 1822 pass, 0 fail. `check_the_world` 0 blocking; `check_the_work` clean. `packs/README.md`'s tally recomputed 92 → 90 and `product-wiki`'s row 8 → 7 (the `catalog-tally` guard holds the aggregate).

{"number":1004,"title":"#974 stranded fielded pack copies: the engine and pack lanes deliver separately, so a renamed engine module breaks the mount mid-converge","body":"Found by forcing Shepherd's converge immediately after #993 merged, which is exactly what that force is for. Shepherd's run went **green** and its stamp **did not move** — [run 32147342762](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/actions/runs/32147342762), PR missingbulb/Shepherd#45 open and `needs-human`:

```
update: engine — needs-human: the converged tree FAILED its self-test
pack-manifests: the pack in packs/core failed to load:
  Cannot find module '.../.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/slots.mjs'
  imported from '.../.claudinite/shared/packs/core/task-declaration-shape.mjs'
```

## What is actually broken

The converged tree carries the **new engine** (`calendar.mjs`, no `slots.mjs`, no `run.mjs`) beside the **old `core` pack**, whose `task-declaration-shape.mjs` still imports `engine/scheduler/slots.mjs`.

That is not a race — it is the standing shape of the delivery model. The engine lane (`updates/engine-update.mjs`) and the pack lane (`updates/pack-update.mjs`) are separate PRs on separate cycles, and pack delivery is version-gated per pack. **There is always a window where a member has the new engine and an old pack**, and nothing can close it.

#974's precondition asked the right question of the wrong callers: *"deleting `run.mjs` strands any member whose workflow still calls it; none does."* True — but a **pack file** importing it strands the same way, and three do. Across every historical pack version the fielded imports are exactly:

| module | symbol | fielded importer |
|---|---|---|
| `slots.mjs` | `FREQUENCIES` | `packs/core/task-declaration-shape.mjs` |
| `run.mjs` | `ensureLabels` | `packs/basics/tasks/task-janitor/worker.mjs` |
| `run.mjs` | `parseOverrides` | `packs/sheepdog/tasks/fleet-digest/worker.mjs` |

The `core` one breaks the **mount** (a pack that fails to load fails the self-test, so the converge refuses to land at all). The other two would break their tasks at runtime.

## The fix

The repo already has this rule for the other direction — *"Changing an export in `updates/*` — empty it, never remove it. Fielded workers are stale callers of instantly-current flow modules"*. This is the same asymmetry one lane over: **fielded pack files are stale callers of an instantly-current engine.**

So `engine/scheduler/slots.mjs` and `engine/scheduler/run.mjs` come back as thin compatibility shims re-exporting only those three symbols, with an expiry condition stated at the definition: they go when no member's `packVersions` still names a version that imports them.

## Done means

- [ ] `slots.mjs` re-exports `FREQUENCIES` from `calendar.mjs`; `run.mjs` re-exports `ensureLabels` from `github.mjs` and `parseOverrides` from the bag parser
- [ ] a test that fails when either shim loses a symbol a fielded pack version imports — quantified over the imports found in git history, not a hand-kept list
- [ ] a guard that catches the general class: a `packs/**` file importing an `engine/**` module that this change deletes or renames
- [ ] Shepherd converges green, stamp moves, and PR missingbulb/Shepherd#45 is superseded
- [ ] only then the `fleet-baseline` `DRY_RUN` #974 still owes

2. **Local-pack `run_daily` scheduling turns on for real.** `readLocalTasks` becomes the planner's *default* `localTasksFor`; every "experimental / not enabled by default / do not pass the seam" statement is purged from the repo. The moved canon-curation tasks are the path's nightly dogfood.

No such directory is ever created: `apply-vendor-set.mjs` materializes the vendor set at **canon-relative** paths, so `engine/hooks/environment-setup-command.sh` lands at `.claudinite/shared/engine/hooks/environment-setup-command.sh`.

The sentence contradicts itself — it links the canon path as `engine/hooks/…` and then names `engine/vendoring/` as where that same file is vendored to.

Verified against a real adoption (missingbulb/Shepherd, canon `599c287`): `ls .claudinite/shared/engine/vendoring/` → no such file or directory; the script is present under `engine/hooks/`. The script's own header agrees — it says it is "vendored into every consumer's `.claudinite/shared/engine/hooks/`".

The cost is that Part 9 is the one step an adopting session hands to a human as a path to go open, so the wrong path survives the session that produced it and lands in whatever issue or note carries the handover. It cost exactly that here before the owner caught it.

Suggested fix — Part 9's second sentence:

> The corpus holds the one generic script — [`engine/hooks/environment-setup-command.sh`](engine/hooks/environment-setup-command.sh), vendored into `.claudinite/shared/engine/hooks/` — identical for every project: paste its full body …

Secondary, same paragraph and same reader: Part 9 describes the script as running `env.mjs install` and the SessionStart step as `env.mjs check`, but the module is `engine/pack_loader/env-requirements.mjs` and the script's line 33 invokes `env-requirements.mjs install`. Part 5's halt-gate bullet carries the same `env.mjs check` spelling. {"number":1126,"title":"Name the summary line in the session-start directive instead of pointing at it","body":"Fixes #1125.

`session-summary.mjs` printed the summary line, then a directive ending in "open your first reply of this session with **that line**". The directive was the last line on stdout, so the nearest line to the reply was the directive itself — and this session opened two replies in a row by reciting it verbatim.

Three properties now make the pick unambiguous, each pinned by the test:

- the directive **disclaims itself** ("an instruction to you, not text to repeat"), so it cannot read as the payload;
- **no deixis** — nothing points at a line the reader has to resolve;
- the summary line is emitted **once**, and **last**, introduced by the directive's colon, so recency now points at the right line rather than the wrong one.

Output is now:

```
SESSION-START SUMMARY — an instruction to you, not text to repeat. Open your first reply of this session with exactly this line, and nothing before it:

Claudinite loaded, 8 packs, 35 checks, 15,000 rule tokens, 23 available skills.
```

The existing test asserted the old deictic wording, so it is rewritten rather than added to — watched red on all four properties before the fix, green after. Nothing outside the loader parses this stdout, so the layout was free to change.

Full suite green apart from the shallow-clone guard in `engine-pack-lane-shims.test.mjs`, which fails loudly by design in this sandbox's history-less checkout. `check_the_world`: 0 blocking.

{"number":934,"title":"A client-side dashboard for a repo's Claudinite task state, past and present","body":"## Problem

There is no single place to see what a repo's Claudinite scheduler is actually doing. Answering "what ran last night, what is stuck, what wakes next" today means reading the issue list by eye, cross-referencing `[claudinite-work]` titles against the task declarations at HEAD, and separately checking the Actions tab. The state exists — it is just spread across three surfaces and none of them is shaped like the queue's own model.

## Proposal

A single-page, **client-side-only** dashboard. No server, no build step, no stored credentials anywhere but the viewer's own browser: the page talks to `api.github.com` with a token the viewer pastes, so the viewer's own GitHub permissions are the entire access-control story.

Renders, for any repo passed as `?repo=owner/name`:

- **Task roster** — one row per declared task (`packs/*/tasks/*`, plus the repo's local packs), with its frequency, model, outcome ceiling, next anchor, and the state of its standing work item.
- **Queue** — open `[claudinite-work]` items by state label (`task:blocked` / `task:ready` / `task:executing` / `task:agent` / `needs-human`), with leash and stale-ready warnings computed from the engine's own thresholds.
- **History** — closed items and their `outcome:*` verdicts over time.
- **Runs** — the scheduler workflow's recent and in-flight Actions runs.

## The one design commitment

**No duplicated vocabulary.** The queue's label set, title grammar, comment markers, leash constants and anchor math are all pure ESM in `engine/scheduler/` with no `node:` imports — so the page imports those modules directly rather than restating them. The dashboard cannot drift from the engine because it has no copy to drift from.

That choice is what sets the hosting answer: ES modules are CORS-checked, so the page needs an `http://` origin rather than `file://`. Any static server over the checkout is enough — no deployment and no GitHub Pages.

## Scope

Lands under `dev/tools/` as a canon-home dev tool, alongside the existing `dev/tools/badges/`. It is repo-parameterized, so it already serves any member; promoting it into a vendored pack is a separate call, not assumed here.

{"number":1060,"title":"Collapse chrome-extension-release into chrome-extension, and stop packs discussing each other","body":"Closes #1057. Four commits: the engine tolerance, the collapse, the reference sweep, and the cross-pack prose purge.

## The design question the issue named

Merging an opt-in release standard into an always-on coding pack looks like it turns the release checks on for every extension repo. It does not, because **the release half's activation was always structural** — `chrome-extension-release`'s `detect` was the orchestrator workflow's name, and declaring the pack was a second copy of that same fact which each repo had to remember to write.

So the fact is now read where it is used: `shipsReleasePipeline` gates the coded rule, all seven `cer/` declared checks carry the same test as their `relevantWhen`, and `store-release`'s precondition asks it of the `release` signal. A repo that only *codes* an extension is asked for no release config, no privacy page and no README release sections. A repo that publishes gets all of it without declaring anything.

**Two signals, either one enough** — the orchestrator's `name:`, or a `.github/release.config`. Each alone leaves the rule that judges it unreachable: gate only on the name and a repo that renamed its orchestrator loses every release check *including the one that tells it to rename it back*; gate only on the config and `cer/release-config`, whose whole job is a missing config, can never fire. The orchestrator is matched by name and never by path, because the canon hosts files at those paths and would otherwise fingerprint itself.

The gate is spelled three times — the coded rule, the JSON (which cannot import), and the scheduler signal (the engine may not import a pack) — so a test runs all three over one matrix of repo shapes and fails if any copy drifts. Seen failing on each copy in turn.

## Members

`RENAMED_PACKS` gains `chrome-extension-release → chrome-extension`, so a member activates the right pack the moment the mount lands, declaration converged or not; a pack-owned record at `chrome-extension` version 3 converges the declaration itself. No engine version bump, so no canary release gate is involved.

The rename **collides on every member**, because the absorbed pack's `requires` meant everyone declaring it declared the survivor too. `applyPackRenames` now merges instead of producing a duplicate: first occurrence keeps its position, its own values win a conflict, arrays union, and an object absorbed into a plain-string entry promotes it. Dropping either side would drop the member's own `config`, `rules` and `accept` — acceptances especially, since a dropped one brings its finding straight back.

**The `cer/` ids do not change**, for the same reason: `accept` entries name rules by id.

## A pack does not discuss its neighbours

Reviewing the collapse turned up the wider class: `firebase-release`'s README opened by saying it is declared "like chrome-extension". A `barriers` probe (`siblings: "packs"` → `packs/*`) found **51 such crossings across 22 packs**, in two shapes:

- **Boundary/turf prose** — "sits under X", "that is Y's turf", a whole `## Boundary` section listing what the neighbours own. Purged. It is a second copy of what `ruleRoutingGuidance.excludes` already carries in one machine-read field — the field the pack directory routes a lesson by — so each site now states what the pack does *not* cover without naming who does.
- **Procedure pointers** — a rule delegating a how-to to another pack's skill, a check's `doc:` field, an executable command, and the comments on the dashboard's deliberate duplicates of sheepdog's helpers. Kept: the link is what makes the procedure findable, and restating it in both places is exactly what the corpus forbids.

22 references survive, all in the second class. No standing barrier rule was added — the probe was a measuring instrument, and it is not in the diff.

## Consumer safety

The shape the collapse newly exposes is an extension repo that codes but does not publish — the canon publishes no extension, so its own CI says nothing about it. `packs-tests/rehearsal/fixtures.mjs` gains that shape (`codes-an-extension`), and a pack test asserts every release rule is inert on it.

## Folders touched

- **`engine/pack_loader/`, `engine/migrations/`** — the rename-map entry and the merge in `applyPackRenames`.
- **`engine/scheduler/signals/`** — the `release` signal carries whether the repo publishes, read off the checkout beside the manifest version it already read.
- **`packs/chrome-extension/`** — absorbs the release module, the seven declared checks (each gated), the stubs, the `store-release` task, both migration records, and `RELEASE.md` as the **`chrome-store-releases`** skill; manifest, README and RULES rewritten for one pack.
- **`packs/firebase`, `firebase-release`, `google-identity`, `jwt`, `web-speech`, `headless-browser`, `executable-requirements`, `spec-driven-product`, `web-scraping`, `git-github`, `sheepdog`, `claudinite-growth`, `claudinite-lifecycle`, `basics`** — neighbour prose removed, and in the release packs' case references to the pack that no longer exists.
- **`.github/`** — the core workflows README, and the retired pre-vendoring release copies' own naming.
- **`packs-tests/rehearsal/`** — the fixture shape above.
- Versions bumped on every pack whose content changed; `packs/directory.GENERATED.md` re-rendered by its test.

The two migration records keep their wording — they describe arrangements true when they were written.

## Verification

- `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` — 2200 pass, 0 fail.
- `check_the_work --changed --base origin/main` — exit 0.
- `check_the_world` — 0 blocking, 61 advisory (all pre-existing).

{"number":1060,"title":"Collapse chrome-extension-release into chrome-extension, and stop packs discussing each other","body":"Closes #1057. Four commits: the engine tolerance, the collapse, the reference sweep, and the cross-pack prose purge.

## The design question the issue named

Merging an opt-in release standard into an always-on coding pack looks like it turns the release checks on for every extension repo. It does not, because **the release half's activation was always structural** — `chrome-extension-release`'s `detect` was the orchestrator workflow's name, and declaring the pack was a second copy of that same fact which each repo had to remember to write.

So the fact is now read where it is used: `shipsReleasePipeline` gates the coded rule, all seven `cer/` declared checks carry the same test as their `relevantWhen`, and `store-release`'s precondition asks it of the `release` signal. A repo that only *codes* an extension is asked for no release config, no privacy page and no README release sections. A repo that publishes gets all of it without declaring anything.

**Two signals, either one enough** — the orchestrator's `name:`, or a `.github/release.config`. Each alone leaves the rule that judges it unreachable: gate only on the name and a repo that renamed its orchestrator loses every release check *including the one that tells it to rename it back*; gate only on the config and `cer/release-config`, whose whole job is a missing config, can never fire. The orchestrator is matched by name and never by path, because the canon hosts files at those paths and would otherwise fingerprint itself.

The gate is spelled three times — the coded rule, the JSON (which cannot import), and the scheduler signal (the engine may not import a pack) — so a test runs all three over one matrix of repo shapes and fails if any copy drifts. Seen failing on each copy in turn.

## Members

`RENAMED_PACKS` gains `chrome-extension-release → chrome-extension`, so a member activates the right pack the moment the mount lands, declaration converged or not; a pack-owned record at `chrome-extension` version 3 converges the declaration itself. No engine version bump, so no canary release gate is involved.

The rename **collides on every member**, because the absorbed pack's `requires` meant everyone declaring it declared the survivor too. `applyPackRenames` now merges instead of producing a duplicate: first occurrence keeps its position, its own values win a conflict, arrays union, and an object absorbed into a plain-string entry promotes it. Dropping either side would drop the member's own `config`, `rules` and `accept` — acceptances especially, since a dropped one brings its finding straight back.

**The `cer/` ids do not change**, for the same reason: `accept` entries name rules by id.

## A pack does not discuss its neighbours

Reviewing the collapse turned up the wider class: `firebase-release`'s README opened by saying it is declared "like chrome-extension". A `barriers` probe (`siblings: "packs"` → `packs/*`) found **51 such crossings across 22 packs**, in two shapes:

- **Boundary/turf prose** — "sits under X", "that is Y's turf", a whole `## Boundary` section listing what the neighbours own. Purged. It is a second copy of what `ruleRoutingGuidance.excludes` already carries in one machine-read field — the field the pack directory routes a lesson by — so each site now states what the pack does *not* cover without naming who does.
- **Procedure pointers** — a rule delegating a how-to to another pack's skill, a check's `doc:` field, an executable command, and the comments on the dashboard's deliberate duplicates of sheepdog's helpers. Kept: the link is what makes the procedure findable, and restating it in both places is exactly what the corpus forbids.

22 references survive, all in the second class. No standing barrier rule was added — the probe was a measuring instrument, and it is not in the diff.

## Consumer safety

The shape the collapse newly exposes is an extension repo that codes but does not publish — the canon publishes no extension, so its own CI says nothing about it. `packs-tests/rehearsal/fixtures.mjs` gains that shape (`codes-an-extension`), and a pack test asserts every release rule is inert on it.

## Folders touched

- **`engine/pack_loader/`, `engine/migrations/`** — the rename-map entry and the merge in `applyPackRenames`.
- **`engine/scheduler/signals/`** — the `release` signal carries whether the repo publishes, read off the checkout beside the manifest version it already read.
- **`packs/chrome-extension/`** — absorbs the release module, the seven declared checks (each gated), the stubs, the `store-release` task, both migration records, and `RELEASE.md` as the **`chrome-store-releases`** skill; manifest, README and RULES rewritten for one pack.
- **`packs/firebase`, `firebase-release`, `google-identity`, `jwt`, `web-speech`, `headless-browser`, `executable-requirements`, `spec-driven-product`, `web-scraping`, `git-github`, `sheepdog`, `claudinite-growth`, `claudinite-lifecycle`, `basics`** — neighbour prose removed, and in the release packs' case references to the pack that no longer exists.
- **`.github/`** — the core workflows README, and the retired pre-vendoring release copies' own naming.
- **`packs-tests/rehearsal/`** — the fixture shape above.
- Versions bumped on every pack whose content changed; `packs/directory.GENERATED.md` re-rendered by its test.

The two migration records keep their wording — they describe arrangements true when they were written.

## Verification

- `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` — 2200 pass, 0 fail.
- `check_the_work --changed --base origin/main` — exit 0.
- `check_the_world` — 0 blocking, 61 advisory (all pre-existing).
- The merge and both drift-guard directions seen red before the code that fixes them; the crossing count re-measured after the purge.

{"number":1106,"title":"Remove the legacy single-integer version tolerance","body":"#1100 moved engine and pack versions to date-anchored `.` and left every reader accepting a legacy positive integer as well, parsed as `.0`. That tolerance was scoped to one week — **from 2026-08-27** — by which point every member converging nightly has re-stamped under the new format. This issue removes it.

**Do not start before 2026-08-27.** Before removing anything, confirm no member still stamps a legacy integer: the fleet roster's mount probe already reads each member's `claudinite.engineVersion` and `packVersions`. If any member does, comment with which ones and re-defer rather than breaking their converge — a stamp the parser rejects reads as "no version installed", which re-applies every migration record in the corpus.

**What to remove**

- `engine/version.mjs` — the number branch of `parseVersion`, `isLegacyVersion`, the `LEGACY TOLERANCE` paragraph, and the `'?` optional-quote groups in the scraper anchors that exist only to read an unquoted integer. `VERSION_SOURCE` tightens to the date-anchored shape.
- The legacy integers still standing in the canon, which are what the tolerance is carrying by then:
  - each pack's `minEngineVersion` floor (`packs/*/pack.mjs`) — a floor at `1` constrains nothing and should go rather than be converted; `claudinite-dashboard` (`4`) and `claudinite-canary-repo` (`3`) are real floors below the oldest engine any live member runs, so they go the same way.
  - every migration record's `version:` range (`engine/migrations/*/`, `packs/*/migrations/*/`). A record whose range predates the format applies to nobody by then; check `migrationApplies` against each member's stamp before deleting one.
- The `PACK_VERSIONED` fixture's legacy spelling in `vendoring/rehearsal/fixtures.mjs`, and the zero/legacy assertions in `engine-tests/version.test.mjs`.

Keep `parseVersion`'s treatment of **zero** — that is the install floor (`docs/versioned-updates/DESIGN.md` §3), not a legacy version.

**Done** when `grep -n "isLegacyVersion\|legacy" engine/version.mjs` is empty, no `version:` or `minEngineVersion:` in the tree is a bare integer, and the full suite plus `check_the_world` are green.

Closes #1566

Comment class: feature

#1565 migrated the shared packs using the rationale their prose still carried. This pass goes after the rationale that earlier compactions had already **deleted** — recoverable only from the change history — and lands it as references entries.

## How the seam was found

Every commit touching a `packs/*/RULES.md`, `packs/*/skills/*/SKILL.md` or a local pack's `RULES.md` across the full (un-shallowed) history, diffed at `-U0`, each removed line attributed to the rule it sat under, and kept only where that rule's bold subject still stands in the tree today. Then, per prose file, the **longest historical version** of every surviving rule against its current text.

One seam dominates: #1315 cut this repo's own local pack to one trigger and directive per rule, and the evidence went with it — 70 of its 165 rules lost text, most of it issue ids, incidents and measurements.

## What landed

`.claudinite/local/packs/claudinite/references.md` gains **64 entries** (`RULES-4` … `RULES-67`), each recovered from the prose the rule carried before the cut; the rules gain their bare `(n)` marker and nothing else. Four bullets my markers pushed past 100 bytes were re-wrapped.

Verified against the source, not just the old prose — a sample read end-to-end: #919 (the `configSchema` seam deleted whole on the owner's call), #959 (the owner's "why do you even need a drift guard? Just write the json" — in that issue's growth-extract provenance comment), #1001, #1004, #1060, #1069, #1106, #1118, #1126, #364, #934, #1275.

One citation did not corroborate as written: the removed prose credited **#952** with the "link the deepest settings URL, don't write out a breadcrumb trail" rule, but #952 is bootstrap Part 9 naming a vendored path that cannot exist. The entry records what #952 actually shows — a hand-written path in the one step a session hands a person survived into the handover — rather than the claim history attached to it.

## What deliberately did not move

- **The shared canon packs have no un-recovered evidence loss.** The four historical removals carrying issue ids or measurements (verify-in-production's executor-batch parks, writing-tests' #429/#310, unattended-agents' worked examples, writing-pack-prose's fenced-command measurement) are already the entries #1565 wrote.
- **The #467-era tightening of the technology packs** (html, node, leaflet, firebase, aws-sam, spec-driven-product, research-project, executable-requirements) removed mechanism detail and restatement, not rationale — converting it would be writing entries, not recovering them.
- Rules whose lost clause was a directive that became its own rule, or a consequence the current text already states, stay unmarked.

## Verification

- Suite `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')`: 2931/2931 pass.
- `check_the_world`: 0 blocking, 87 advisory — unchanged from `main`, none introduced.
- `references-integrity` silent on the real tree, and seen firing on a deliberately dangling `(99)` marker before restoring.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files, comment-only changes, and history-keeping updates (a version bump, a changelog or `VERSIONS.md` row).
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and author the canon packs those facets earn. ---
name: merge-to-main
description: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
---

# Merge to main

If the project's own `CLAUDE.md` names a merge-policy file, that file overrides the divergent
points below (merge method, CI gating). Don't go hunting for one it doesn't name.

1. Load `create_pull_request` + `merge_pull_request` in one `ToolSearch`.
2. No PR open for the branch? `create_pull_request` (base `main`), body ending `Closes #<issue>`.
3. If the PR has check runs, wait for them to pass. None — merge without waiting.
4. `merge_pull_request`, `merge_method: squash`, title `<subject> (#<pr>)`. Don't pre-read
   mergeability; the call fails loudly.
5. Sync local `main`: `git checkout main && git pull origin main`.
6. Capture the conversation:
   `node .claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`
   (in the canon repo: `node packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`). Skip only if
   the repo doesn't declare `claudinite-growth`. A later merge in the same session runs it again.
7. Run the basics pack's
   [verify-in-production](../../../basics/skills/verify-in-production/SKILL.md) skill, unasked.
   This step is that skill's **only** trigger — it files against what the squash actually landed,
   which is why it runs here and not when the code was written or the PR opened. It decides
   whether this change needs a production check at all — most don't — and files the issue that
   comes back once the change is live. Never offer the owner to check later instead.

Don't re-read the issue to confirm it closed — `Closes #<issue>` does that on merge.

- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
